Are we relying too heavily on containerized infrastructure to secure autonomous AI agents?

As multi-agent coordination expands and agents run real commands on development machines, system-level security and sandbox architectures are becoming essential requirements for production workflows.

Here are the key technical developments from today across AI tooling, benchmarks, and agent frameworks:

🔒 Anthropic open-sourced sandbox-runtime (srt), the OS-level sandbox powering Claude Code. Rather than using traditional Docker containers, it applies native OS security mechanisms—Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux—to restrict file system and network access for AI agents, MCP servers, and CLI tools.

🐝 Microsoft Research open-sourced Agensh, a multi-agent harness built without a central orchestrator. Self-organizing worker agents share a Git repository, chat channels, and a findings board to collaborate, successfully scaling from 1 to 1,024 agents on ProgramBench under a strict 6-hour time budget.

📊 Five Qwen3.8-27B models managed to match the performance of Fable 5 when benchmarked together using the GVS5H harness setup.

🛑 OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly blocked the Reserve Engineer Anything (REA) project, an automated tool designed to reverse engineer smart TVs spying on user networks, with Claude enforcing blocks one day after release.

These developments reflect a clear architectural shift toward kernel-level agent isolation, decentralized worker coordination, and stricter provider restrictions around automated reverse engineering.

Which approach do you prefer for securing local AI agent execution: heavy containerization or native OS-level sandboxing?
